title: There Are Plenty of Reasons to Be Concerned About Bioweapons Development—Even Without AI
gist: Michael Mechanic interviews Annie Jacobsen about her book Biological War: A Scenario. She argues bioweapons are the greatest overall WMD threat because the barrier to entry is low, and that accidental leaks from the world's roughly 3,600 BSL-3/BSL-4 labs are statistically far more likely than deliberate attacks. Pentagon war-gamers conclude there is no real defense against a large-scale biological attack. Anthropic's misuse report on Claude gain-of-function queries is used to frame AI as further lowering the barrier, though her book deliberately leaves AI out.

insights.claim: Anthropic published a misuse report detailing five cases in which foreign scientists tried to get around Claude's guardrails on gain-of-function questions; Anthropic refused the answers and cut off the accounts while noting their motives may not have been sinister.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: AI labs are actively enforcing biosecurity guardrails, a growing compliance cost and a likely subject of regulation for frontier model providers.
insights.locator: That last one isn’t merely theoretical.

insights.claim: Gain-of-function information is inherently dual-use: the same knowledge that could enhance a pathogen also helps scientists develop vaccines and drugs, which makes AI guardrails hard to calibrate.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Overly strict guardrails could hurt AI usefulness in biotech R&D, while lax ones bring liability and regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Like so many technologies, AI included, genetic engineering can be used for both good and evil.

insights.claim: Jacobsen deliberately left AI out of her book to show that, even without AI, a lab scientist can tweak natural pathogens into a near-extinction-level pandemic; her sources' concern that AI lowers the barrier further was 'not even a question'.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Bio risk is not primarily an AI problem, so AI-focused regulation alone will not neutralize it.

insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Public salience of AI bio risk could unlock funding and policy for biodefense and countermeasures.

themes.theme: Low barrier makes bio the top WMD threat

insights.claim: A Defense Department WMD threat spectrum ranks biological weapons a close second to nuclear in destructiveness, and Jacobsen argues they are the greatest overall threat because the barrier to entry is extremely low and attacks are therefore more likely.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Biodefense deserves strategic priority close to nuclear deterrence, a tailwind for countermeasure spending.
insights.quote: the threshold for entry is extremely low, and therefore it is more likely to happen.
insights.locator: The Defense Department document that I reprinted

insights.claim: Nuclear weapons require state-level capabilities (fissile material, ICBMs, bombers, submarines) and are held by nine states, while potential pandemic agents are accessible to most of the world.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Bio proliferation cannot be contained by state-focused arms control, which raises the tail risk of non-state attacks.

insights.claim: Advances in genetic engineering, gain-of-function research and AI-enabled bio mean pathogens can now be engineered to evade existing immunity (as in the mousepox experiment) or become airborne (as in the H5N1 ferret experiments), putting 'everything on the table' for pandemic potential.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Engineered pandemic risk is rising structurally, which strengthens the long-term case for pandemic preparedness assets.
insights.quote: We are in a completely different world now.

insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: State bioweapons programs are a persistent geopolitical tail risk tied to great-power rivalry.

insights.claim: Accidental release is a much greater threat than deliberate use because there are about 3,600 BSL-3 and BSL-4 labs worldwide manipulating pathogens, far more than terrorist groups, while intelligence agencies actively disrupt terrorist bio programs.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Biosafety regulation of high-containment labs is the main lever, and a lab-leak event is the likeliest pandemic tail risk.
insights.quote: There are not 3,600 terrorist organizations that I am aware of. So the chance for an accident is statistically far greater.

insights.claim: Because a bioweapon is likely to come back on its creator, any deliberate release would most likely come from a non-state actor with a death wish, such as the ecoterrorists in the Glade X planning exercise who engineered Nipah virus.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: State deterrence logic does not apply to the most plausible deliberate attackers.

insights.claim: Researchers working on high-risk pathogens tend to default to publishing and pursuing gain-of-function work, which the author and Jacobsen view as hubris that discounts the risk of catastrophic release.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Growing skepticism of gain-of-function research could tighten funding and publication restrictions.
insights.locator: I studied to be a molecular biologist

insights.claim: Retired Air Force Colonel Tom Ehrhard, who ran Pentagon catastrophic war games for the Office of Net Assessment, concluded there is no real defense against a large-scale biological attack, only mitigation.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Mitigation assets such as countermeasures, stockpiles and detection are the investable response, not prevention guarantees.
insights.quote: There is no real defense against a large-scale biological attack, only things you can do to mitigate extermination.

insights.claim: US planning for a catastrophic bio event expects anarchy from fear of infection and scarce countermeasures, leading to the Insurrection Act, continuity-of-government condition COGCON 1, and a classified 'devolution' plan that sends pre-selected individuals to bunkers to reconstitute government.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Government planning assumes social order breaks down, a reminder of the systemic tail risk from shortages of medical countermeasures.
insights.locator: I did not know that. Devolution

insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Pandemic scenarios carry migration and security spillovers that planners take seriously.

insights.claim: Pneumonic plague is airborne with a near-100% case fatality rate, and engineering away antibiotic effectiveness turns a 'disease of the past' back into an existential threat, which Jacobsen frames as a metaphor for dual-use science, like AI.
insights.speaker: Michael Mechanic
insights.so_what: Antimicrobial resistance, engineered or natural, is an underpriced biosecurity risk.
